title: Diesel Engines
summary: Diesels have no spark plugs: they squeeze air until it is hot enough to ignite fuel injected at very high pressure. See why that makes them efficient and torquey, and why they need glow plugs, turbochargers and elaborate exhaust cleaning.
learningObjectives: Explain compression ignition and how it differs from spark ignition
Describe how a diesel controls power without a throttle
Outline common-rail injection and the role of pilot injections
Name the main diesel exhaust after-treatment devices and what each removes
beginnerExplanation:
Squeeze air quickly and it gets hot — you can feel this in a bicycle pump. A diesel engine squeezes air so hard that it becomes hotter than the temperature at which diesel fuel ignites by itself. Fuel is then sprayed into that hot air near the top of the piston's travel, and it starts burning straight away without any spark.

A diesel has no throttle valve choking the air supply. It always takes in a full breath of air, and the driver's foot simply controls how much fuel is injected. Avoiding the throttle and using very high compression are the two big reasons diesels use less fuel than similar petrol engines.

The downsides come from how the fuel burns. Diesel combustion produces soot and nitrogen oxides, so modern diesels carry filters and catalysts in the exhaust, sometimes topped up with a urea solution (AdBlue). Cold starts need help too: glow plugs pre-heat the combustion chambers so the first compression strokes get hot enough.
technicalExplanation:
Modern road diesels use compression ratios of about 15:1 to 18:1 (older indirect-injection engines ran higher). Near top dead centre the trapped air reaches several hundred degrees Celsius, above the auto-ignition temperature of diesel fuel. Fuel injected at that moment evaporates and ignites after a short ignition delay; fuel with a higher cetane number ignites more readily. Fuel that accumulates during the delay burns suddenly, which causes the characteristic diesel knock, so common-rail systems fire one or more small pilot injections first to start combustion gently before the main injection.

Load is controlled by fuel quantity rather than air quantity ('quality control'), so the engine runs overall lean — λ is well above 1 at part load — and avoids throttling losses. High compression gives a high expansion ratio, extracting more work from each charge. Peak efficiency of a modern passenger-car diesel is typically around 40–45%. Nearly all are turbocharged because a diesel can accept boost without knock; the limit is smoke, peak cylinder pressure and exhaust temperature.

A common-rail system stores fuel at roughly 1,600–2,500 bar in a shared rail; solenoid or piezo injectors open several times per cycle under ECU control. Because combustion happens in locally rich and locally hot zones, the engine produces particulates and NOx. After-treatment typically includes a diesel oxidation catalyst (CO, HC), a diesel particulate filter that traps soot and periodically burns it off (regeneration), exhaust gas recirculation to lower combustion temperatures, and selective catalytic reduction where injected urea forms ammonia that converts NOx to nitrogen and water.

steps.title: Fill with air only
steps.beginner: The piston moves down and draws in a full charge of air — no fuel yet, and no throttle restricting it.
steps.technical: Unthrottled intake (often boosted by a turbocharger and cooled by an intercooler) maximises trapped air mass and avoids pumping losses.

steps.title: Compress until hot
steps.beginner: The piston squeezes the air into a tiny space, and it becomes hot enough to ignite fuel on its own.
steps.technical: At around 16:1 compression the near-adiabatic temperature rise takes the charge well above diesel's auto-ignition point. Glow plugs assist when the block is cold.

steps.title: Inject at high pressure
steps.beginner: Just before the piston reaches the top, fuel is sprayed in as an extremely fine mist.
steps.technical: Common-rail injectors deliver pilot, main and sometimes post injections at 1,600–2,500 bar; fine atomisation shortens ignition delay and improves mixing.

steps.title: Burn and push
steps.beginner: The fuel ignites as it meets the hot air, and the expanding gas pushes the piston down.
steps.technical: Combustion is mixing-controlled: heat release rate follows how quickly fuel and air mix, so injection rate shaping directly controls pressure rise and noise.

steps.title: Clean the exhaust
steps.beginner: Filters and catalysts remove soot and harmful gases before the exhaust leaves the car.
steps.technical: Oxidation catalyst → particulate filter (with periodic regeneration) → SCR catalyst dosed with urea; EGR reduces NOx formation upstream.

keyConcepts.definition: Fuel ignites because the air it is injected into is already hotter than the fuel's auto-ignition temperature.
Cylinder volume with the piston at the bottom divided by the volume with it at the top.
Diesel power is set by how much fuel is injected into an unthrottled air charge, so the engine runs lean at part load.
A measure of how readily a diesel fuel auto-ignites; higher cetane shortens ignition delay and softens combustion noise.

misconceptions.myth: Diesels make more torque because diesel fuel is far more powerful.
misconceptions.reality: Diesel holds only roughly 10–15% more energy per litre than petrol. The torque comes mainly from turbocharging, high cylinder pressures and efficient, unthrottled operation.

misconceptions.myth: A diesel needs a spark to start when cold.
misconceptions.reality: There is no spark at all. Glow plugs simply heat the chamber so compression can reach ignition temperature in a cold engine.

misconceptions.myth: A blocked particulate filter means the engine is broken.
misconceptions.reality: Usually the filter has not had a chance to regenerate. Regular short trips never get the exhaust hot enough; a longer steady drive often lets it clear.

practicalExamples: A dashboard coil symbol that lights before starting a cold diesel shows the glow plugs pre-heating.
A diesel used only for short urban trips may show a particulate-filter warning; a sustained run at motorway speed lets it regenerate.
Diesel tractors and lorries rev low but pull hard: long strokes, turbocharging and high cylinder pressure suit heavy, steady loads.

quiz.prompt: What ignites the fuel in a diesel engine?
options: The glow plug on every cycle
quiz.explanation: The air is compressed until it is hotter than the fuel's auto-ignition temperature; glow plugs only help cold starts.

quiz.prompt: How does a diesel engine mainly control its power output?
options: By varying the amount of fuel injected
quiz.explanation: Diesels run unthrottled and vary fuel quantity, which avoids pumping losses and is a key reason for their efficiency.

quiz.prompt: What does a selective catalytic reduction (SCR) system with urea dosing remove?
quiz.explanation: Urea decomposes to ammonia, which reacts with NOx over the SCR catalyst to form nitrogen and water.
